before: Carpal tunnel syndrome is one of the most common repetitive strain injuries in the American workplace, affecting millions of workers whose jobs require repetitive hand and wrist movements. If your job caused or significantly contributed to your carpal tunnel syndrome, you may be entitled to workers' compensation benefits in both Georgia and South Carolina — including medical treatment, wage replacement, and compensation for any permanent impairment. However, carpal tunnel claims are among the most frequently disputed workers' compensation cases because insurers often challenge whether the condition is truly work-related. The Cornell Law Institute provides a useful overview of workers' compensation law as it applies to occupational diseases and repetitive stress injuries.
after: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a very common nerve condition, and jobs that demand the same forceful hand and wrist motions over and over can cause or worsen it. If your job caused or significantly contributed to your carpal tunnel syndrome, you may be entitled to workers' compensation benefits in both Georgia and South Carolina — including medical treatment, wage replacement, and compensation for any permanent impairment. However, carpal tunnel claims are among the most frequently disputed workers' compensation cases because insurers often challenge whether the condition is truly work-related. The Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute provides a useful overview of workers' compensation law.

before: Unlike traumatic injuries that result from a single accident, carpal tunnel syndrome typically develops gradually over weeks, months, or years of repetitive hand and wrist activity. This makes it an occupational disease or repetitive motion injury under workers' compensation law — a category that requires the worker to establish a connection between their job duties and the development of the condition.
after: Unlike traumatic injuries that result from a single accident, carpal tunnel syndrome typically develops gradually over weeks, months, or years of repetitive hand and wrist activity. This makes it a repetitive trauma injury — in South Carolina a category with its own statute (S.C. Code § 42-1-172), and in Georgia a gradual work injury rather than an occupational disease. Either way, the worker must establish a connection between their job duties and the development of the condition.

before: Georgia's Workers' Compensation Act, codified in Title 34, Chapter 9 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, covers occupational diseases including carpal tunnel syndrome when the condition arises out of and in the course of employment.
after: Georgia's Workers' Compensation Act, codified in Title 34, Chapter 9 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, covers carpal tunnel syndrome as a gradual work injury when it arises out of and in the course of employment (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1(4)).

before: Georgia requires injured workers to report their injury to their employer within 30 days under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80. For repetitive motion injuries like CTS, the 30-day clock generally starts when the worker knows or should know that their condition is work-related — which may be when a doctor first diagnoses the condition as being connected to work duties, rather than when symptoms first appear.
after: Georgia requires injured workers to report their injury to their employer within 30 days under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80. For carpal tunnel that builds up while you keep working, Georgia generally dates the injury to when the condition forces you to stop working. Do not wait for that: report symptoms to your supervisor in writing as soon as you suspect your job is the cause. Late notice may be excused if your employer already knew, or if you had a reasonable excuse and the employer was not prejudiced.

before: Workers must file a claim with the Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation within one year of the last date of exposure to the hazardous condition or within one year of the date the worker became aware that the condition was work-related, under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82.
after: Workers must file a claim with the Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation within one year of the injury — for gradual carpal tunnel, usually the day the condition forces you to stop working, which Georgia courts treat as a "fictional new accident" (Central State Hosp. v. James, as quoted in Donnelley v. Ogletree (2011)). The deadline extends to one year from the last employer-paid treatment, or two years from your last weekly income benefit (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82).

before:
Georgia Comparative Fault Note

Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 in personal injury cases, barring recovery at 50% or more fault. However, workers' compensation is a no-fault system — your own actions do not bar your claim. Even if you could have used better ergonomic practices, you are still entitled to benefits if your work duties caused or contributed to your CTS.
after:
Georgia No-Fault Rule

Workers' compensation is a no-fault system — your own carelessness does not bar your claim; only narrow exceptions do, such as willful misconduct, refusing to use a required safety device, or intoxication (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17). Even if you could have used better ergonomic practices, you are still entitled to benefits if your work duties caused or contributed to your CTS.

before: South Carolina's workers' compensation system, governed by Title 42 of the South Carolina Code, also covers occupational diseases including carpal tunnel syndrome.
after: South Carolina's workers' compensation system, governed by Title 42 of the South Carolina Code, also covers carpal tunnel syndrome as a repetitive trauma injury, decided only under S.C. Code § 42-1-172: the work link must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence through a physician's opinion stated to a reasonable degree of medical certainty.

before: South Carolina requires workers to report their injury to their employer within 90 days under S.C. Code § 42-15-20. This more generous timeline compared to Georgia provides additional time for workers with gradually developing conditions like CTS to recognize and report their symptoms.
after: South Carolina requires workers to report their injury to their employer within 90 days under S.C. Code § 42-15-20. For repetitive trauma, the 90 days do not start until you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, that your condition was compensable (S.C. Code § 42-15-20(C)).

before: The statute of limitations for filing a workers' compensation claim in South Carolina is two years from the date of injury or the last date of exposure under S.C. Code § 42-15-40.
after: For carpal tunnel and other repetitive trauma injuries, you must file a claim with the Workers' Compensation Commission within two years after you knew or should have known the injury was compensable — and no later than seven years after your last injurious exposure at work (S.C. Code § 42-15-40).

before: If you reach MMI with a permanent impairment rating, you are entitled to permanent partial disability benefits. Both Georgia and South Carolina use scheduled loss provisions for hand and wrist impairments, with benefits calculated based on the impairment rating assigned by your treating physician.
after: If you reach maximum medical improvement (MMI) with a permanent impairment rating, you are entitled to permanent partial disability benefits. Both states pay them on a schedule — in Georgia, up to 160 weeks for the total loss of use of a hand and 225 weeks for an arm; in South Carolina, 185 weeks for a hand and 220 weeks for an arm — multiplied by the percentage of impairment (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263; S.C. Code § 42-9-30).

before: If your CTS prevents you from returning to your former job, you may be entitled to vocational rehabilitation services to help you transition to a new position. This is particularly important for workers whose entire career has involved the type of repetitive hand work that caused the condition.
after: Georgia's workers' comp system must provide vocational rehabilitation only for catastrophic injuries (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1), and South Carolina's has no rehabilitation benefit — but the Georgia and South Carolina vocational rehabilitation agencies offer retraining to workers who cannot return to their former jobs. This is particularly important for workers whose entire career has involved the type of repetitive hand work that caused the condition.

before:
• "Not work-related" — The most common defense, arguing that the CTS was caused by non-work activities, hobbies, or pre-existing medical conditions rather than job duties.
  • "Pre-existing condition" — Arguing that the worker had CTS before beginning the current job. However, even if a pre-existing condition existed, workers' compensation covers aggravation of pre-existing conditions when work duties make it worse.
  • "Late reporting" — Claiming the worker did not report the condition within the required timeframe. This defense is often used because CTS develops gradually, and workers may not realize they should report it until symptoms become severe.
  • "Insufficient medical evidence" — Challenging the adequacy of the medical evidence connecting CTS to work duties, often by retaining their own medical experts who disagree with the treating physician.
  • "No objective findings" — Arguing that the diagnostic testing does not support the diagnosis, particularly when nerve conduction studies show borderline results.

before:
Recovery from carpal tunnel surgery typically takes several weeks to several months. Workers usually cannot return to full duty for 4-6 weeks after surgery, and those who must perform repetitive hand work may require even longer before reaching maximum recovery. During this recovery period, workers' compensation should cover all medical expenses and provide temporary disability wage benefits.

After surgery, some workers may have permanent restrictions that prevent them from returning to their previous job. In these cases, the worker may be entitled to permanent disability benefits and vocational rehabilitation services to transition to a position that does not aggravate the condition.
after:
Recovery from carpal tunnel surgery typically takes several weeks to several months. Your surgeon decides when you can return to work and with what restrictions; according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, grip and pinch strength usually return in about 2 to 3 months, but can take 6 to 12 months if the nerve was badly compressed. During this recovery period, workers' compensation should cover authorized medical treatment and provide temporary disability wage benefits.

After surgery, some workers may have permanent restrictions that prevent them from returning to their previous job. In these cases, the worker may be entitled to permanent disability benefits and help from the state's vocational rehabilitation agency to transition to a position that does not aggravate the condition.

before: Carpal tunnel can qualify as an occupational disease in Georgia and South Carolina. How to prove it is work-related, and when to report it.
after: Carpal tunnel can qualify for workers' comp in Georgia and South Carolina as a repetitive work injury. How to prove it is work-related, and when to report it.

before: Carpal tunnel syndrome qualifies for workers' compensation in both Georgia and South Carolina as an occupational disease. Georgia requires reporting within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and filing within one year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). South Carolina allows 90 days for reporting (S.C. Code § 42-15-20) and two years for filing (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Workers' comp is no-fault — pre-existing conditions and employee actions do not bar claims.
after: Carpal tunnel syndrome can qualify for workers' compensation in both Georgia and South Carolina as a repetitive work injury — South Carolina requires medical evidence of the work link (S.C. Code § 42-1-172). Georgia requires reporting within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and filing within one year of the injury, with extensions after employer-paid treatment or income benefits (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). South Carolina allows 90 days to report and two years to file, both measured from when you knew or should have known your carpal tunnel was work-related and compensable, with a seven-year outer limit for filing (S.C. Code §§ 42-15-20, 42-15-40). Workers' comp is no-fault — carelessness does not bar a claim, and work that aggravates a pre-existing condition can still be covered.

before: Benefits include full medical treatment (doctor visits, therapy, surgery), temporary total or partial disability wage replacement (typically two-thirds of your average weekly wage), permanent partial disability compensation if you have lasting impairment, and vocational rehabilitation if you cannot return to your former job.
after: Benefits include authorized medical treatment (doctor visits, therapy, surgery), temporary total disability (two-thirds of your average weekly wage, up to $800 a week in Georgia for injuries on or after July 1, 2023, and $1,189.94 in South Carolina for 2026 accidents) or partial disability (two-thirds of the wage difference), and permanent partial disability compensation if you have lasting impairment. Vocational rehabilitation is a Georgia comp benefit only for catastrophic injuries and is not part of South Carolina's system.
